name: Classic-Style Test 2
source: Original questions written for LSAT Trainer in the style and difficulty of recent LSATs. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: Psychologist: Among the 600 adults we surveyed, those who regularly sing in a choir reported feeling lonely far less often than those who do not. So joining a choir is an effective way for a person to reduce loneliness.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the psychologist's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: draws a conclusion about adults in general from a survey of only some adults
overlooks the possibility that people who are seldom lonely are more inclined to join a choir
takes for granted that singing in a choir is the only way to reduce loneliness
fails to consider that some choir members may still feel lonely on occasion
confuses how often people feel lonely with how intensely they feel lonely
questions.explanation: The argument moves from a correlation (choir singers report less loneliness) to a causal claim (joining reduces loneliness) without ruling out reversed causation: people who are already less lonely may be the ones who join choirs, which is (B). (A) is tempting, but nothing suggests a 600-person survey is unrepresentative; the problem is the causal leap, not the sample. (C) and (D) attribute claims the argument never makes.

questions.stimulus: Real estate agent: A house priced far below similar homes nearby is seldom the bargain it appears to be. Sellers rarely set a low price without a reason, and that reason is often a defect, such as a cracked foundation or a history of flooding, that an ordinary walkthrough will not reveal. Admittedly, some sellers simply need to sell quickly. But a buyer has no way of knowing which kind of seller he or she is dealing with.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the conclusion drawn in the real estate agent's argument?
choices: Sellers who set an unusually low price usually do so because the house has a hidden defect.
Some sellers price their houses low because they need to sell quickly.
A buyer cannot tell whether a low price reflects a hidden defect or a seller's haste.
A house priced far below similar nearby homes is unlikely to be a genuine bargain.
Buyers should have every low-priced house professionally inspected before making an offer.
questions.explanation: Everything after the first sentence supports it: sellers have reasons for low prices, the reason is often a hidden defect, and the possibility of a merely hasty seller is neutralized because buyers cannot tell the difference. So the conclusion is (D). (C) is the tempting choice, but it is the final premise that answers the concession, not the point being argued for; (A) overstates 'often' as 'usually', and (E) recommends something the agent never says.

questions.stimulus: Entomologist: In the orchards of the Varrow Valley, the population of the native orange-banded bee has fallen sharply over the past decade, the same period during which growers there widely adopted a new fungicide. Although the fungicide is not designed to affect insects, I believe it is responsible for the bees' decline.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the entomologist's argument?
choices: In valley orchards never treated with the fungicide, orange-banded bee numbers have held steady.
The new fungicide controls orchard fungi more effectively than the products it replaced.
Orange-banded bees visit orchard blossoms less often than several other bee species do.
Over the past decade, a parasitic mite that attacks orange-banded bees has spread throughout the valley.
Some growers in the valley have recently begun planting wildflowers to attract bees.
questions.explanation: The argument rests on a coincidence in timing between the fungicide's adoption and the bees' decline. (A) supplies a comparison: where the fungicide was absent, the bees did not decline, which makes the fungicide a more likely cause. (D) is relevant to the topic but points to an alternative cause, so it weakens rather than strengthens; (B), (C), and (E) do not bear on what caused the decline.

questions.stimulus: The town of Merriton has two pharmacies, and they charge nearly identical prices for prescription drugs. Yet Hollins Pharmacy, which is open only on weekdays, fills far more prescriptions each month than Cardale Pharmacy, which is open seven days a week and stays open later each evening.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why Hollins Pharmacy fills more prescriptions than Cardale Pharmacy despite keeping shorter hours?
choices: Cardale Pharmacy employs more pharmacists than Hollins Pharmacy does.
Most prescriptions in Merriton are filled on weekday afternoons.
Hollins Pharmacy is in the same building as the clinic where most Merriton residents see their doctors.
Cardale Pharmacy also sells groceries and household goods.
Some Merriton residents have their prescriptions filled by mail-order services rather than at either pharmacy.
questions.explanation: We need some advantage of Hollins that outweighs Cardale's longer hours and equal prices. (C) supplies one: patients leaving the clinic with a prescription can fill it in the same building. (B) is tempting, but both pharmacies are open on weekday afternoons, so it removes Cardale's advantage at most without giving Hollins one; (A) and (D) make the gap more puzzling, and (E) affects both pharmacies equally.

questions.stimulus: Meteorologist: Our station's new forecasting model correctly predicted whether it would rain the next day on 88 percent of days last spring. The model we used before was correct on only 74 percent of days during the previous spring. So the new model predicts next-day rain more accurately than the old one did.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the meteorologist's argument?
choices: The new model will be correct on at least 88 percent of days next spring.
The old model was more accurate in spring than in any other season.
No forecasting model available to the station is more accurate than the new model.
The new model requires less computing time than the old model did.
Next-day rain last spring was not substantially easier to predict than it was during the previous spring.
questions.explanation: The models were tested in different springs, so the comparison works only if the two springs posed similar forecasting challenges. If last spring's weather was much easier to forecast, the higher score would not show that the model is better; that is (E). (A) is not required, because the conclusion concerns the model's accuracy so far, not a guarantee about next spring; (C) concerns other models, which the argument never compares.

questions.stimulus: At Quillon Software, an employee may work from home on a given day only if that employee's team lead has approved it in advance. Team leads approve such requests only from employees who have completed the company's security training. Moreover, an employee working from home may not access the customer database that day unless he or she uses the company's encrypted connection.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Any Quillon employee who has completed the security training may work from home whenever he or she requests it.
Any Quillon employee who works from home on a given day has completed the company's security training.
Every Quillon employee who uses the encrypted connection is working from home.
Quillon's team leads approve most of the requests to work from home that they receive.
A Quillon employee who uses the encrypted connection need not have a team lead's approval to work from home.
questions.explanation: Working from home requires advance approval, and approval is given only to employees who have completed the training, so anyone working from home has completed it: (B). (A) reverses the rules, treating completed training as enough to secure working from home rather than as a requirement. (C) likewise reverses the encrypted-connection rule, and (E) contradicts the first rule.

questions.stimulus: Archaeologist: At the hilltop site of Tel Varo, we found grinding stones together with charred barley grains in a layer dated to about 9,000 years ago. Since grinding stones were used to process grain, the people who lived at Tel Varo must already have been farming barley at that time.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the archaeologist's argument?
choices: Grinding stones found at other sites in the region are older than those found at Tel Varo.
The charred barley grains at Tel Varo were dated using a highly reliable method.
Later layers at Tel Varo contain clear evidence of cultivated barley.
Wild barley grew abundantly in the region 9,000 years ago, and people elsewhere ground wild grain long before farming began.
Barley is easier to grind than most other cereal grains.
questions.explanation: The evidence shows that people at Tel Varo ground barley, but the conclusion is that they farmed it. (D) shows that the evidence fits equally well with gathering and grinding wild barley, so it does not establish farming. (C) may look relevant because it mentions cultivated barley, but evidence of farming in later layers says nothing about whether farming had begun 9,000 years ago; (B) supports the premise.

questions.stimulus: Editor: A publisher should reissue an out-of-print book only if the author, or the author's estate, consents to the reissue and any factual errors discovered in the book since its first publication can be corrected in the new edition.
questions.stem: The principle stated by the editor most helps to justify the reasoning in which one of the following arguments?
choices: Grayline Press should not reissue Owen Tarr's travel memoir. Although Tarr's estate favors a reissue, the original plates cannot be altered, so the errors found in the memoir could not be corrected.
Hollis Books should reissue Meera Dahl's first novel. Dahl has consented to the reissue, and no factual errors have been found in the novel since it first appeared.
Fenwick House should not reissue its 1970s cookbook, since the original edition sold poorly and there is little reason to expect a reissue to sell better.
Arden Press should reissue Lionel Fry's chemistry textbook. Its errors have now been corrected, and that matters more than Fry's objection to the reissue.
Lattice Press should not reissue Ana Voss's field guide, because Voss has died and much of the information in the guide is now out of date.
questions.explanation: The principle states only necessary conditions for reissuing: consent and the ability to correct errors. It therefore can justify a decision not to reissue when one condition fails, as in (A), where errors exist and cannot be corrected. (B) is the trap: both conditions are met, but meeting necessary conditions does not show that a book should be reissued. (E) fails because Voss's estate might consent and outdated information might be corrected; (D) violates the consent requirement.

questions.stimulus: Firefly species attract mates with species-specific patterns of flashes. Females of a few predatory firefly species, however, mimic the flash patterns of other species' females, luring males of those species and then eating them. The mimics tend to make small timing errors when they repeat a pattern, so males of prey species that respond only after watching a female's signal several times are eaten less often than males that respond at once. Thus, ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: the females of prey species repeat their signals several times in order to help males avoid predators
males of prey species cannot distinguish the signals of their own females from those of the mimics
where such mimics are common, prey males that delay their responses probably survive at higher rates
the predatory mimics reproduce flash patterns more accurately than the females they imitate do
most males of prey species that live near the mimics are eaten before they have a chance to mate
questions.explanation: Males that wait are eaten less often, and that difference matters most where mimics are common, so delaying males should survive at a higher rate there: (C). (A) is attractive, but nothing indicates why females repeat their signals, let alone that they do so to protect males. (B) contradicts the claim that watching repetitions helps males avoid mimics, (D) contradicts the timing errors, and (E) is far stronger than the evidence.

questions.stimulus:
Kemal: The city's new rule limiting short-term rentals in residential neighborhoods will lower rents. Many apartments now rented to tourists will return to the long-term market, and that added supply will push rents down.

Rosa: The rule will indeed send some apartments back to long-term tenants. But there will be too few to lower rents noticeably. Most of the city's short-term rentals are spare rooms in owner-occupied houses, and their owners will simply stop renting them out.
questions.stem: The dialogue most strongly supports the claim that Kemal and Rosa agree that
choices: the rule will noticeably lower rents in the city
most of the city's short-term rentals are rooms in owner-occupied houses
the city should not have adopted the rule limiting short-term rentals
owners of short-term rentals will mostly oppose the city's new rule
the rule will lead some apartments now rented to tourists to become available to long-term tenants
questions.explanation: Kemal says apartments will return to the long-term market, and Rosa says 'indeed' some will, so both accept (E). (A) is exactly what they disagree about. (B) is Rosa's claim alone, since Kemal says nothing about spare rooms, and neither speaker evaluates the rule, as (C) requires, or predicts owners' opposition, as (D) requires.

questions.stimulus: Pharmacist: Whenever a generic version of a drug becomes available, our pharmacy stocks it, provided that our suppliers can deliver it reliably. Our suppliers can reliably deliver any drug that is made in a facility that passed its most recent national inspection. A generic version of the asthma drug Brelomax has just become available. So our pharmacy will stock generic Brelomax.
questions.stem: The pharmacist's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Generic Brelomax is made in a facility that passed its most recent national inspection.
Our suppliers can reliably deliver only drugs made in facilities that passed their most recent national inspections.
The brand-name version of Brelomax is made in a facility that passed its most recent national inspection.
Our pharmacy stocks no generic drug that our suppliers cannot deliver reliably.
Generic Brelomax is as effective as the brand-name version of the drug.
questions.explanation: The chain is: made in an inspected facility, therefore reliably deliverable; available and reliably deliverable, therefore stocked. The only missing link is that generic Brelomax comes from an inspected facility, which (A) supplies. (B) and (D) reverse the conditionals, turning sufficient conditions into necessary ones, so neither establishes that the drug will be stocked. (C) concerns the wrong version of the drug.

questions.stimulus: Media critic: Some newspapers now let readers vote online on which stories receive follow-up coverage. Supporters claim that this practice makes journalism more responsive to the public. In fact, it is likely to make journalism less responsive. The readers who bother to vote are mostly those already devoted to a few favorite topics, so the stories chosen will tend to reflect the interests of a small, unrepresentative group rather than those of the public at large.
questions.stem: The claim that the stories chosen will tend to reflect the interests of a small, unrepresentative group plays which one of the following roles in the media critic's argument?
choices: It is the argument's main conclusion.
It is a claim made by supporters of the practice that the argument seeks to refute.
It is a premise offered in support of the claim that the readers who vote are mostly devoted to a few topics.
It is a conclusion supported by another claim in the argument and offered in support of the main conclusion.
It is a concession that the critic argues is irrelevant to the main conclusion.
questions.explanation: The critic's main conclusion is that the practice is likely to make journalism less responsive. The claim in question follows from the premise about who votes (note the 'so') and in turn explains why responsiveness will decline, making it an intermediate conclusion: (D). (A) is the tempting trap because the claim is the last sentence, but it serves the claim that the practice will make journalism less responsive. (C) reverses the direction of support.

questions.stimulus: Tech analyst: Brightway Software is the most profitable company in its industry. Therefore Brightway's tablet division, although it brings in only a small share of the company's revenue, must also be more profitable than the tablet divisions of Brightway's competitors.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the tech analyst's reasoning?
choices: It relies on a comparison between companies that operate in different industries.
It confuses a company's revenue with its profitability.
It presumes that what is true of a company as a whole is true of each of its parts.
It takes for granted that a company's most profitable division brings in most of its revenue.
It fails to consider that Brightway's competitors may become more profitable in the future.
questions.explanation: Brightway's profitability as a whole is used to draw a conclusion about one division, though a profitable company can include an unprofitable division: (C). (B) is tempting because revenue is mentioned, but the argument never treats revenue as profit; it mentions revenue only to note that the division is small. (E) concerns the future, which the argument does not address.

questions.stimulus: In the coastal city of Pellmouth, the number of summer days on which the temperature exceeds 35°C has risen steadily over the past thirty years. Over the same period, however, the number of people admitted to Pellmouth's hospitals each summer for heat-related illness has fallen.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain how heat-related hospital admissions in Pellmouth could have fallen while very hot days became more common?
choices: The temperature in Pellmouth rarely exceeds 35°C for more than three days in a row.
Over the past thirty years, the proportion of Pellmouth homes with air conditioning has risen from under one-fifth to nearly nine-tenths.
Heat-related illness is more common among elderly people than among younger people.
Inland cities near Pellmouth have had an even larger increase in the number of very hot days.
Most heat-related hospital admissions in Pellmouth occur on days when the temperature exceeds 35°C.
questions.explanation: We need a change over the thirty years that reduced residents' vulnerability to heat even as heat increased. The large rise in air conditioning in (B) does exactly that. (C) is tempting, but it explains the decline only if Pellmouth's population had grown younger, which is not stated; (E) deepens the puzzle, and (A) describes a pattern with no change over time.

questions.stimulus: Archaeologist: Pottery from the ancient settlement of Ombra bears a distinctive spiral motif that has been found at only one other site in the region, the coastal settlement of Dessin, two hundred kilometers away. The earliest spiral-decorated pottery at Dessin is about a century younger than the earliest at Ombra. So people from Ombra probably settled at Dessin.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions most helps in evaluating the archaeologist's argument?
choices: Did the people of Ombra decorate objects other than pottery with spirals?
How many pieces of pottery in total have been excavated at Ombra?
Was Ombra a larger settlement than Dessin at the height of its population?
Did the people of Dessin continue to use the spiral motif after Ombra was abandoned?
Was the spiral-decorated pottery found at Dessin made from clay found near Dessin or from clay found near Ombra?
questions.explanation: The pottery could have reached Dessin through trade rather than through settlers from Ombra. If the Dessin pots were made of Ombra clay, trade becomes likely and the argument weakens; if they were made locally, someone at Dessin knew Ombra's style, supporting settlement. So (E) helps evaluate the argument either way. (D) is tempting, but continued use of the motif at Dessin fits both settlement and later imitation, so neither answer settles much.

questions.stimulus: Psychologist: A therapist should not tell a client that a treatment will work when the evidence shows only that it often works. Overstating a treatment's prospects may persuade a client to begin it, but a client who later finds the promise broken will be less willing to trust the therapist at the times when that trust matters most.
questions.stem: The principle underlying the psychologist's argument is most similar to the principle underlying which one of the following arguments?
choices: A doctor should tell patients about every possible side effect of a medication, since patients surprised by side effects may stop taking it.
A salesperson should not exaggerate a product's benefits, because doing so is dishonest whether or not customers are ever harmed by it.
A coach should not assure an athlete that a training plan guarantees a team spot; the promise may motivate now, but if it proves false, the athlete will heed the coach less when it counts.
A teacher should praise students' efforts rather than their results, because students who are praised for effort tend to work harder.
A manager should not promise an employee a raise that she lacks the authority to grant, since her own supervisors may then penalize her for committing the company without permission.
questions.explanation: The psychologist's principle: do not overstate the likely benefit of a course of action to get someone to adopt it, because the broken promise will erode the trust you will need later. (C) matches on every element, including the overstatement, the short-term persuasion, and the later loss of trust. (B) is the trap: it condemns the same kind of exaggeration but justifies the condemnation by dishonesty alone, not by its effect on future trust. (E) rests on harm to the promiser rather than lost trust.

questions.stimulus: Pharmacy analyst: Last year Medway Pharmacies began sending a text message to customers who had opted in to the service whenever one of their prescriptions was due for a refill. Among those customers, the proportion of refills picked up on time rose from 61 percent the year before to 78 percent. The messages, therefore, were responsible for the rise.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the analyst's argument?
choices: Among Medway customers who did not opt in, the on-time refill rate last year was about the same as the year before.
In a survey, most customers who received the messages described them as helpful and said they hoped the service would continue.
Before the messages began, customers who later opted in had already been picking up refills on time somewhat more often than other customers.
Last year several competing pharmacies in the area closed, and many of their customers began using Medway.
The text messages also announced discounts on nonprescription products sold at Medway.
questions.explanation: The argument infers causation from a before-and-after change in one group, so it is vulnerable to a general trend (such as a change in insurance rules) that raised on-time refills for everyone. (A) supplies a control: customers who got no messages showed no rise, which makes the messages the likelier cause. (C) is the most tempting trap, but the comparison is of the same customers before and after, so their higher starting rate does not bear on what caused the rise. (B) offers only customers' impressions, which say little about whether the messages changed their behavior.

questions.stimulus: Developer: Apartment rents in downtown Ferrisport have risen 30 percent in just three years, while many of the downtown office buildings nearby now stand largely empty. Converting those empty office buildings into apartments would therefore be a profitable investment.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the developer's argument?
choices: Apartment rents in Ferrisport's suburbs have risen less over the past three years than downtown rents have.
Converting the downtown office buildings would require running new plumbing to every unit, at a cost exceeding what the apartments could earn in rent for decades.
Several of the empty downtown office buildings were built within the last fifteen years.
Ferrisport's downtown population has grown faster than its supply of housing.
Some office tenants have left downtown Ferrisport for cheaper space in the suburbs.
questions.explanation: High rents and empty buildings show that converting could earn revenue, but profitability also depends on cost. (B) shows that the conversion costs would outweigh decades of rent, undercutting the conclusion directly. (D) strengthens the case for demand, and (A), (C), and (E) do not affect whether the conversions would pay off.

questions.stimulus: Entomologist: On the island of Tavor, every ant species that cultivates fungus keeps the interior of its nests humid. Most of the island's ant species that keep their nests humid build those nests underground, and none of Tavor's ant species that nest underground forage at night. Several ant species on Tavor do forage at night.
questions.stem: If the entomologist's statements are true, which one of the following is most strongly supported by them?
choices: None of Tavor's fungus-cultivating ant species forage at night.
Some of Tavor's ant species that forage at night cultivate fungus.
Most of Tavor's fungus-cultivating ant species build their nests underground.
Most of Tavor's ant species that keep their nests humid do not forage at night.
Several of Tavor's fungus-cultivating ant species forage at night.
questions.explanation: Most humid-nest species nest underground, and no underground nesters forage at night, so most humid-nest species do not forage at night: (D). (C) is the main trap. Fungus cultivators are only a subset of the humid-nest species, and that subset could fall entirely within the minority that nests above ground, so what holds for most humid-nest species need not hold for most fungus cultivators. For the same reason, (A), (B), and (E) are all left open.

questions.stimulus: Newspaper editor: Over the past five years, our paper has lost half of its readers under the age of thirty. Young people increasingly get their news from short online videos. So if we begin producing short news videos of our own, we will win back many of the young readers we have lost.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the editor's argument depends?
choices: Producing short news videos is the only way for the paper to win back young readers.
Most young people prefer short online videos to every other source of news.
Producing short news videos will not cost more than the paper can afford.
The young readers the paper has lost stopped reading it because they began getting their news from short videos.
Some of the young readers the paper has lost would watch short news videos produced by the paper.
questions.explanation: The editor predicts that the paper's videos will win back lost young readers, which cannot happen unless some of those particular readers would watch the paper's videos. Negate (E) and the prediction collapses. (D) is the attractive trap: those readers might have left for other reasons and still watch the paper's videos, so the argument does not need it. (C) concerns whether the plan is advisable, not the prediction actually made, and (A) and (B) are far stronger than required.

questions.stimulus: Ethicist: When the software firm Lumetra discovered a security flaw in its messaging app, it fixed the flaw within a week but chose not to tell users, on the grounds that there was no evidence the flaw had ever been exploited. Lumetra acted wrongly. People who sent sensitive messages during the months the flaw existed had a stake in knowing that those messages might have been exposed, even though they probably were not.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, would most help to justify the ethicist's argument?
choices: A company should tell users about a security flaw in its product whenever there is evidence that the flaw has been exploited.
A company should fix any security flaw in its products as soon as the flaw is discovered.
Whether users are owed disclosure of a risk depends on what they had at stake, not just on how likely the risk was to materialize.
A company that conceals a security flaw from users acts wrongly only if the concealment results in actual harm to those users.
People who send sensitive messages through an app accept responsibility for the risks of doing so.
questions.explanation: The ethicist rejects Lumetra's reasoning, which was that disclosure was unnecessary because exploitation was unlikely, and argues that users' stake in the information required disclosure anyway. (C) makes users' stake, rather than the probability of exposure, the deciding factor, which licenses the conclusion. (A) is the tempting trap: it requires disclosure when there is evidence of exploitation, but here there was none, so it does not apply to Lumetra's case. (D) and (E) cut against the ethicist.

questions.stimulus: Most of the novels that Starling House published last year were by first-time novelists. Most first-time novelists whose books were published last year received advances of less than $5,000. So most of the novels Starling House published last year earned their authors advances of less than $5,000.
questions.stem: The pattern of questionable reasoning in the argument above is most similar to that in which one of the following?
choices: Most cars Dunmore Motors sold last month were electric. Most electric cars sold in the region last month cost over $40,000. So most cars Dunmore sold last month cost over $40,000.
Most of the plants in the Hadley greenhouse are orchids. Every orchid in the greenhouse requires daily misting. So most of the plants in the Hadley greenhouse require daily misting.
Most members of the Orrin hiking club are retirees. Most of the club's retirees hike every week. So at least some members of the Orrin hiking club hike every week.
Most residents of Calder own bicycles. Most residents of Calder own cars. So some residents of Calder own both a bicycle and a car.
Most applicants to the Velor fellowship are from Varn. Most of the fellowship's recipients are from Varn. So most applicants from Varn receive the fellowship.
questions.explanation: The argument applies a fact about first-time novelists in general to Starling's first-time novelists, though Starling's could be the minority who received large advances. (A) makes the same move: Dunmore's electric cars might be the cheaper minority of the region's electric cars. (B), (C), and (D) are attractive because they also combine 'most' statements, but each is valid: (B) uses 'every', (C) restricts the second premise to the club's own retirees, and two majorities of the same group must overlap in (D). (E) is flawed in a different way, inferring a high success rate from where most applicants and recipients come from.

questions.stimulus: Archaeologist: Any ancient structure aligned precisely with the sunrise on the summer solstice was built by people who tracked the sun's yearly movements over many years. People who tracked the sun's movements over that long a period must have kept some form of lasting record. The stone ring at Hallow Fen is aligned precisely with the summer solstice sunrise. Therefore, the builders of the Hallow Fen ring possessed a system of writing.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the archaeologist's argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Any people who possessed a system of writing kept lasting records of the sun's movements.
The builders of the Hallow Fen ring tracked the sun's yearly movements over many years.
Most ancient structures aligned with the summer solstice sunrise were built by people who possessed a system of writing.
Any people who kept a lasting record of any kind possessed a system of writing.
Some ancient people who kept lasting records of the sun's movements possessed a system of writing.
questions.explanation: The premises establish that the ring's builders kept some form of lasting record; the conclusion requires that they had writing. (D) bridges that gap: anyone who kept any lasting record had writing. (A) reverses the needed conditional. (C) and (E) are tempting because they link alignment or record-keeping to writing, but 'most' and 'some' cannot guarantee that these particular builders had writing. (B) merely restates something the premises already establish.

questions.stimulus: Climatologist: Of the severe storms that struck the Lundar coast over the past decade, 70 percent were preceded by a week of unusually warm temperatures in the adjacent sea. Hence, whenever the sea off the Lundar coast has a week of unusually warm temperatures, a severe storm will probably follow.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the climatologist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: treats a correlation between two kinds of events as proof that one kind of event causes the other
infers that one kind of event is usually followed by a second kind from evidence that the second is usually preceded by the first
draws a general conclusion from data covering too short a period of time
fails to consider that some severe storms occur after weeks of normal sea temperatures
presumes that unusually warm sea temperatures are the only factor that can produce a severe storm
questions.explanation: That most storms were preceded by warm weeks does not show that most warm weeks were followed by storms; warm weeks could be common and storms rare. The argument reverses the direction of the proportion, which is (B). (A) is the very tempting trap, but the conclusion is a prediction ('will probably follow'), not a causal claim, so the argument's error lies elsewhere. (D) describes something the premise itself acknowledges (the other 30 percent), and a decade of data, as in (C), is not the problem.

questions.stimulus: Pharmacist: When our patients are switched from a brand-name drug to a cheaper generic version, a substantial minority call within the first week to ask whether the generic will work as well. Such calls are far less frequent when the generic pill has the same color and shape as the brand-name pill, even though the generic contains the identical active ingredient in either case.
questions.stem: The pharmacist's statements, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Generic pills that look different from the corresponding brand-name pills are less effective than those that look the same.
Patients are less likely to take a generic drug as directed when it looks different from the brand-name pill.
Pharmacies should dispense only generic drugs that resemble the brand-name drugs they replace.
Most patients who are switched to a generic drug do not notice the change.
Some patients' doubts about a generic drug's effectiveness are influenced by something other than its active ingredient.
questions.explanation: Calls are less frequent when the pill looks the same, even though the active ingredient is identical either way, so something other than the ingredient, namely the pill's appearance, affects whether patients doubt the drug: (E). (A) is tempting but unsupported; the pharmacist reports patients' doubts, not differences in effectiveness, and in fact implies the drugs are the same. (B) goes beyond calls to whether patients take the drug as directed, and (C) adds a recommendation the facts do not support.

passages.title: Participatory Budgeting
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
Passage A

Participatory budgeting—the practice of letting residents vote directly on how a portion of a city’s capital budget will be spent—has spread widely since its origins in Brazil in the late 1980s, and its advocates describe it as a remedy for civic disengagement. Yet the arrangement raises at least three problems that its enthusiasts have been slow to confront.

First, those who take part are not a fair sample of the city. Proposal meetings, at which residents decide which projects will appear on the ballot, are typically held on weeknight evenings, and they reward residents who have flexible schedules, reliable child care, and the confidence to speak in public. A process meant to widen participation can thus hand still more influence to the residents who already have the most.

Second, the process is biased toward the visible. Residents asked to choose among projects predictably favor new playgrounds, murals, and bike lanes—things they can point to—over replacing aging water mains or resurfacing roads that will merely stop deteriorating. Over time, a city that allocates money this way may find its least glamorous infrastructure starved.

Third, participatory budgeting blurs accountability. When a poorly chosen project fails, voters cannot easily hold anyone responsible: council members can say that residents chose it, and residents chose it as a crowd. A representative system has many faults, but it at least lets citizens identify whom to remove.

Passage B

When the city of Brennick set aside 2 percent of its capital budget for residents to allocate directly in 2014, skeptics predicted that the process would be captured by the same handful of activists who dominate every public hearing. The record of the program’s first eight cycles tells a different story. Because Brennick accepted ballots by mail and at libraries and grocery stores over a two-week period, the share of votes cast by residents of its lowest-income neighborhoods has exceeded those neighborhoods’ share of the city’s population in every cycle.

Nor has the program crowded out the city’s ordinary obligations. Residents decide only how the set-aside is spent; the remaining 98 percent of the capital budget, including every dollar for water and sewer systems, is still allocated by the council. And the projects residents have chosen, far from being frivolous, have often addressed problems that city engineers had overlooked—a dangerous pedestrian crossing near a senior center, for example, that had never appeared in a traffic study because no one had yet been killed there.

Perhaps the program’s most important effect, however, is on the participants themselves. Residents who have spent weeks weighing the cost of a new streetlight against that of a repaired sidewalk come away with a far clearer sense of the trade-offs that every budget involves. Officials who dismiss such programs as symbolic because they control only a sliver of the budget are measuring them by the wrong yardstick: the size of the sums at stake rather than what residents learn in deciding how to spend them.

passages.title: Dark Eggs of the Kessin Sandpiper
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
For shorebirds that nest on open ground, egg color is usually the best defense. In most ground-nesting shorebirds, egg color closely matches the sand or pebbles of the nesting site, and experiments with artificial eggs confirm that well-matched eggs are found by gulls and foxes far less often than mismatched ones. The Kessin sandpiper is a striking exception. Its breeding range runs some 2,000 kilometers from temperate coastal marshes to subarctic gravel plains, and its eggs grow steadily darker toward the north—even though the pale gravel of the northern sites makes dark eggs especially easy for predators to spot.

The ornithologist Teodora Valk has proposed that the eggs’ darkness is an adaptation not for concealment but for warmth. Only the female Kessin sandpiper incubates, and because her mate does not feed her, she must leave the nest repeatedly each day to forage. While she is away, the eggs cool, and an embryo whose temperature falls below about 26°C stops developing until it is warmed again. Every such pause lengthens the incubation period, and every extra day that eggs remain in the nest is another day on which a predator or a storm can destroy them. Dark shells absorb more sunlight than pale ones and so slow the eggs’ cooling. Where breeding-season air is cold, Valk contends, this benefit is large enough that the darkness pays for itself, despite the eggs’ greater visibility.

The arithmetic is clearest at a northern colony Valk studied, where air temperatures during incubation averaged 8°C and females’ foraging trips averaged about 25 minutes. Exposed to sunlight, a pale egg there cooled from its incubation temperature of 36°C to the 26°C threshold in about 15 minutes, so on a typical trip its embryo spent roughly 10 minutes with development halted. Over the 60 or so trips of a full incubation, those pauses added up to about 10 hours. A dark egg under the same conditions took about 28 minutes to reach the threshold—long enough, on most trips, to avoid any pause at all. At the southern end of the range, by contrast, where air temperatures averaged near 20°C, even pale eggs took more than an hour to cool to 26°C; there, darkening would buy no developmental time while still making eggs easier to find.

Two further observations support Valk’s account. First, egg darkness tracks breeding-season temperature more closely than it tracks latitude: of two colonies lying at the same latitude, one on a cold, wind-scoured island and the other in a sheltered inland valley, the island colony lays markedly darker eggs. Second, in northern colonies, nests with darker clutches hatched more often overall than nests with paler ones, even though, day for day, darker clutches were found by predators somewhat more often. Valk’s account leaves some questions open—it does not explain why some northern females lay paler clutches than their neighbors—but it turns what looked like a lapse in camouflage into the predictable result of a trade-off between two dangers.

passages.title: Solvang and the honest seam
passages.text:
In The Honest Seam (1987), the architectural critic Henrik Solvang argued that when a damaged historic building is repaired, the new work should be plainly distinguishable from the old in material, tooling, or color, so that a visitor can “read the building’s wounds.” Imitative repair, which reproduces lost parts in their original manner, Solvang regarded as a quiet forgery: it presents as the testimony of one age what is in fact the product of another. His model was the chapel at Brekke, gutted by fire in 1944 and rebuilt in the 1950s with replacement limestone of a slightly cooler gray and vault ribs left deliberately unmolded. His view soon became orthodoxy among conservation architects.

What Solvang fails to clarify is what “the old” is from which new work must be distinguished. Few buildings reach us in a single state. The Brekke chapel itself had received a new west front in the 1720s and a new roof in the 1860s, yet the 1950s repairs were set off against all earlier fabric alike, as though the 1720s front were as original as the medieval nave. The seam Solvang praises is thus one cut among many, singled out chiefly because it is the most recent. His doctrine, in effect, requires only the latest intervention to announce itself.

The doctrine also rests on two undefended assumptions. It assumes that the principal relationship between a building and the people around it is evidentiary: the building is a document, and its public consists of visitors who come to read it. And it assumes that a distinction, once made, will remain visible. At Brekke, the second assumption has not held. The cooler limestone has weathered within forty years to a near match with the surrounding stone, and the seam that was meant to testify now needs a guide to point it out.

Other complications are harder still. Some building traditions treat faithful reproduction as continuity rather than deceit. The Ise Grand Shrine in Japan has for centuries been rebuilt in the same form at intervals of roughly twenty years; to insist that each rebuilding look different would be to mistake what is being preserved, which is a practice of making rather than a particular set of timbers. The stave barns of the Vestmark valley have been repaired board by board by the farmers who work them, for whom a barn is a tool to be kept in working order rather than a record to be consulted. And a conspicuous seam can mislead in its own way: a viewer who sees a sharp break may infer a catastrophe where there was only routine maintenance.

None of this shows that imitative repair is always right. Solvang was correct that a repair makes a claim about the past, and that such claims can be false. But whether a given repair deceives depends on what the building is understood to be, whether document, instrument, or continuing practice, and that question must be answered before the question of seams can be.
