passages.title: Calder’s rolling beach easement
passages.text:
Along the coast of the province of Calder, the public has long held a customary right to use the dry-sand beach, the strip between the high-water line and the line of permanent vegetation, even where that strip lies on privately titled land. The right was clear enough so long as the coast stayed put. But Calder’s shore moves. When erosion pushes the vegetation line inland, does the public’s easement move with it, onto ground that was formerly a lawn or a house lot, or does it stay fixed and vanish into the sea?

The Calder High Court answered in Ostrander v. Coastal Lands Board (1979). Borrowing from the older law of river boundaries, the court distinguished erosion, a gradual and imperceptible loss of land, from avulsion, a sudden and perceptible loss such as that caused by a single storm. The easement follows gradual change, so a beach that creeps inland over decades carries the public’s right with it. But when a storm abruptly strips away the dunes, the easement remains where it was, and the newly exposed sand stays private unless natural processes rebuild the beach to its former position. Thus an owner whose dune line retreated thirty meters in one hurricane could fence the exposed sand, whereas a neighbor who lost the same thirty meters over twenty years could not.

Ostrander drew criticism from several directions. Landowners argued that a rolling easement shifted the burden of public use onto land they had never surrendered. Public access advocates raised a more practical objection: if most land loss on Calder’s coast occurs in storms, the avulsion exception would swallow the rule, and within a generation fences would line the shore. Coastal geologists, for their part, doubted that the distinction could be applied at all, since much apparently gradual retreat is the cumulative work of many small storms, while a single storm’s losses are often partly reversed as sand returns in the following months. Judge Imelda Corran, dissenting, wrote that the majority had “imported a distinction made for rivers that move their channels to a shore that moves its sand.”

Later developments lent support to these critics. A provincial survey in 1996 found that in counties with frequent storms, owners had fenced more than a third of the formerly public dry beach, and that much of the fenced sand had in fact partly rebuilt on its own. In Reyes v. Port Allard (2011), the court abandoned the speed-based test. It now asks only whether a shift in the vegetation line has persisted for five years: if it has, the easement moves to the new line however the shift occurred; if the line returns seaward within that period, nothing changes.

The Reyes test has critics of its own, who call the five-year period arbitrary. But it has an evidentiary virtue that Ostrander lacked: it asks courts to determine where a line has stood, not to reconstruct how quickly it got there.
passages.subject: law

questions.stem: Which one of the following pairs of titles would most likely be found on documents whose relationship to each other is most analogous to the relationship between passage A and passage B?
choices: “In Defense of Open Admission” and “Three Problems with Open Admission”
“Three Problems with Open Admission” and “Three Problems with Selective Admission”
“Three Problems with Open Admission” and “Open Admission at Harlow College: What a Decade of Results Shows”
“The Origins of Open Admission” and “Open Admission at Harlow College: What a Decade of Results Shows”
“Three Problems with Open Admission” and “Why Harlow College Ended Its Experiment with Open Admission”
questions.explanation: Passage A lists numbered problems with participatory budgeting; passage B defends the practice largely through one city’s track record, which matches C’s critique followed by a case-based defense. A is the tempting trap: it has the right two kinds of document but in the reverse order. B makes the second document a critique of a different practice, D mischaracterizes passage A as a history of origins, and E makes the second document a story of failure rather than a defense.

questions.stem: According to passage A, residents choosing among proposed projects tend to favor projects that
choices: produce results residents can readily see
cost the least to complete
benefit their own neighborhoods
have been endorsed by council members
repair or replace existing infrastructure
questions.explanation: The second problem in passage A is that residents ‘predictably favor’ playgrounds, murals, and bike lanes, ‘things they can point to,’ which is A. E reverses the point: passage A says such repairs, like replacing water mains, lose out. C may sound realistic, but passage A never says residents favor their own neighborhoods, and B and D are not mentioned.

questions.stem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over whether
choices: participatory budgeting began in Brazil
the times at which participatory budgeting events are held affect who takes part
council members can avoid responsibility for projects that residents chose
allocating funds through participatory budgeting tends to divert money from basic infrastructure such as water systems
taking part in participatory budgeting gives residents a clearer understanding of budgetary trade-offs
questions.explanation: Passage A warns that a city using this process ‘may find its least glamorous infrastructure starved,’ naming water mains; passage B replies that every dollar for water and sewer systems is still allocated by the council, so the program ‘has not crowded out’ ordinary obligations. That is D. B is tempting, but passage B’s account of Brennick’s mail and library voting suggests that it accepts the point that access shapes turnout. A, C, and E are each discussed in only one passage.

questions.stem: The author of passage B mentions the pedestrian crossing near a senior center (middle of the second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that residents generally rank safety projects above aesthetic ones
support the claim that residents’ choices can address needs that professional planners have missed
illustrate the kind of project the council funds from the remaining 98 percent of the budget
suggest that city engineers are less competent than residents at identifying hazards
give an example of a visible project of the kind that residents tend to prefer
questions.explanation: The crossing is the example (‘for example’) for the claim that residents’ projects ‘have often addressed problems that city engineers had overlooked,’ which is B. D overstates this into a general comparison of competence, and A generalizes one example into a ranking of priorities that passage B never gives. E borrows passage A’s concern with visible projects, but passage B offers the example to show the projects are not frivolous, not to illustrate a taste for the visible.

questions.stem: The author of passage B suggests that the officials mentioned in the last sentence of passage B are too
choices: generous
deferential
impatient
sentimental
narrow
questions.explanation: Passage B says these officials judge the programs by ‘the wrong yardstick,’ looking only at the size of the sums at stake and ignoring what residents learn. That means their standard of value is too narrow, which is E. ‘Impatient’ (C) may tempt because the officials dismiss the program, but nothing suggests they judged it too soon. The other words have no support.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is a criticism that the author of passage A would be likely to offer regarding the suggestion in passage B that Brennick’s program has not been captured by an unrepresentative group of residents?
choices: Accepting ballots by mail makes it harder to verify that each ballot was cast by an eligible resident.
Figures on who cast ballots reveal little about who took part in deciding which proposals appeared on the ballot.
Even a representative body of voters cannot be held responsible when a project it chose turns out badly.
Eight budget cycles are too few to establish that a pattern of participation will persist.
Residents of low-income neighborhoods are as likely as other residents to favor projects they can point to.
questions.explanation: Passage A’s first problem concerns the proposal meetings, ‘at which residents decide which projects will appear on the ballot,’ which favor residents with free time and confidence. Passage B’s evidence covers only who voted, so passage A would object that turnout figures leave untouched the stage it worries about. That is B. C is the strongest trap: it is passage A’s third problem, but it concedes rather than challenges that the voters were representative. D is a generic objection that passage A gives no basis for, and A and E concern issues passage A never raises about representativeness.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately characterizes the relationship between the two passages?
choices: Passage A raises several objections to a practice; passage B presents evidence that bears against some of those objections and identifies a benefit of the practice that passage A does not discuss.
Passage A raises several objections to a practice; passage B responds in turn to each of those objections, using evidence from a single city.
Passage A traces the origins of a practice; passage B evaluates the results of that practice in one city.
Passage A argues that a practice should be abandoned; passage B argues that the practice should be greatly expanded.
Both passages criticize a practice, but passage B confines its criticism to the version of the practice adopted in one city.
questions.explanation: Passage B answers passage A’s worries about unrepresentative participation and neglected infrastructure, and then adds a benefit passage A never mentions: what participants learn about trade-offs. That is A. B is the trap: passage B never addresses passage A’s third problem, accountability, so it does not respond to ‘each’ objection. C mistakes passage A’s opening mention of Brazil for its purpose, D attributes recommendations neither passage makes, and E misreads passage B as a criticism.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: In ground-nesting shorebirds, egg color serves mainly to conceal eggs from predators by matching the color of the nesting site.
Valk’s measurements prove that dark eggs cool more slowly than pale ones in every shorebird species that nests in cold regions.
Kessin sandpiper eggs are darker in the north because the gravel at northern nesting sites is darker than the sand of southern marshes.

The northward darkening of Kessin sandpiper eggs, though it makes them easier for predators to find, is plausibly explained as an adaptation that limits the developmental pauses caused by cooling while the female forages.
Because only the female incubates, the Kessin sandpiper suffers higher rates of nest loss than shorebird species in which both parents share incubation.
questions.explanation: The passage presents the puzzle of northern eggs that are dark despite pale gravel, then sets out Valk’s warming theory with a worked example and supporting evidence. D states that whole arc. A describes only the general pattern in the first paragraph that the sandpiper breaks. B overstates the claim (‘prove,’ ‘every species’), C contradicts the passage’s statement that northern gravel is pale, and E makes a comparison the passage never draws.

questions.stem: According to the passage, at the southern end of the Kessin sandpiper’s range
choices: dark eggs are found by predators more often than they are in the north
females’ foraging trips are shorter than those of northern females
even pale eggs take more than an hour to cool to the temperature at which embryonic development stops
all of the species’ eggs are pale enough to match the surrounding sand exactly
air temperatures during incubation average about 8°C
questions.explanation: The third paragraph states that in the south, where the air averages near 20°C, ‘even pale eggs took more than an hour to cool to 26°C,’ the threshold at which development stops. That is C. D is tempting because southern eggs are paler, but the passage never says they are uniformly pale or match exactly. E gives the figure for the northern colony, and A and B compare things the passage never measures.

questions.stem: In using the phrase “pays for itself” (end of the second paragraph), the author most probably means that
choices: producing dark pigment costs the female no more energy than producing pale shells does
dark eggs require the female to spend less total time incubating them
the dark color of the eggs eventually makes them harder for predators to see as the season progresses
the food the female gathers while foraging supplies the materials needed to darken the shells
in cold regions, the protection from developmental delay that dark shells provide outweighs the added risk that they will be detected
questions.explanation: The sentence weighs ‘this benefit,’ slower cooling and therefore fewer developmental pauses, against ‘the eggs’ greater visibility,’ and says the benefit is large enough to justify it. That is E. A reads ‘pays’ as a literal metabolic cost, which the passage never discusses. B may tempt, since fewer pauses shorten incubation, but the phrase concerns weighing a benefit against a predation cost, and the passage says nothing about the female’s time on the nest.

questions.stem: The author mentions the two colonies “lying at the same latitude” (fourth paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that egg darkness varies with the factor Valk’s theory emphasizes rather than merely with geographic position
suggest that predators are more numerous on islands than in sheltered inland valleys
provide the figures used in the worked example of the third paragraph
identify a case that Valk’s theory has not yet been able to explain
indicate that females at island colonies take longer foraging trips than those inland
questions.explanation: Two colonies at the same latitude but with different temperatures lay eggs of different darkness. This shows that darkness tracks breeding-season temperature, the variable Valk’s theory depends on, rather than position on the map. That is A. D is tempting because the paragraph does mention an open question, but that question concerns pale clutches among northern neighbors, not these two colonies. B and E invent differences the passage never mentions, and C misplaces the example.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most call into question Valk’s theory mentioned in the second paragraph?
choices: At northern colonies, dark eggs are found by predators more often than pale eggs would be at the same sites.
Females at southern colonies take foraging trips that are, on average, somewhat longer than those of northern females.
Several shorebird species that nest alongside the Kessin sandpiper in the north lay pale eggs, and in those species both parents take turns incubating.
Among northern colonies, eggs are no darker at sites where skies are usually clear during the breeding season than at sites that are overcast through most of it.
The pigment that darkens Kessin sandpiper eggs requires the female to use energy that she must replace by foraging.
questions.explanation: The theory’s mechanism is that dark shells ‘absorb more sunlight’ and so cool more slowly; the worked example concerns eggs ‘exposed to sunlight.’ If darkness is equally pronounced where there is little sun to absorb, the trait does not track the benefit the theory says explains it, so D undermines the theory. A is the main trap, but greater visibility is a cost the theory already acknowledges and weighs. C actually fits the theory, since species where both parents incubate seldom leave eggs uncovered. Even longer southern trips (B) would be far shorter than the hour pale eggs take to cool there, and E names a small cost without challenging the trade-off.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information in the passage?
choices: The darkest Kessin sandpiper eggs are laid at the colonies farthest north in the species’ range.
If females at the northern colony Valk studied typically returned to the nest in less than 15 minutes, dark eggs there would offer little or no developmental advantage over pale ones.
Over a full incubation at the northern colony Valk studied, the embryo in a dark egg would spend no time at all with its development halted.
Kessin sandpiper eggs that are left uncovered in cold air for more than 15 minutes do not hatch.
At the southern end of the range, females spend less time away from the nest each day than females in the north do.
questions.explanation: At the northern colony a pale egg takes about 15 minutes to cool to the 26°C threshold. If trips were shorter than that, pale eggs would never reach the threshold, so dark shells would gain no developmental time, which is B. A is the strongest trap: eggs darken toward the north, but the fourth paragraph says darkness tracks temperature more closely than latitude, so the darkest eggs need not come from the farthest-north colonies. C is too strong, because dark eggs avoid a pause only ‘on most trips.’ D confuses a halt in development with failure to hatch, and E compares something the passage never measures.

questions.stem: The author’s attitude toward Valk’s theory can best be described as
choices: skepticism about the mechanism on which the theory relies
detached neutrality between the theory and the concealment view it challenges
unreserved enthusiasm for a theory regarded as settling the matter
reluctant acceptance of a theory that conflicts with established findings
favorable regard tempered by acknowledgment that some questions remain unanswered
questions.explanation: The author says that two observations ‘support Valk’s account’ and credits it with turning an apparent lapse into a predictable result. The author also notes that it ‘leaves some questions open,’ which is the mix in E. C ignores that caveat. D is tempting, but the author shows no reluctance, and the theory accepts rather than conflicts with the finding that matched eggs are better concealed. A and B do not fit the author’s explicitly supportive language.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Solvang’s doctrine should give way to a general policy of imitative repair, which better respects the traditions within which many buildings were made and maintained.
Because new materials weather to match old ones, distinguishable repair cannot be sustained over time, and Solvang’s doctrine therefore defeats itself.
Solvang’s requirement that repairs be visibly distinct rests on an undefended conception of what a building is, and whether a repair deceives cannot be settled until that conception is.
Since few buildings reach us in a single state, conservation architects should abandon the notion of original fabric altogether.
Solvang rightly holds that repairs make claims about the past, but the rebuilding of the Brekke chapel was a poor application of his own doctrine.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph concedes Solvang’s core insight but concludes that whether a repair deceives depends on what the building is understood to be, a question his doctrine skips, which is C. B inflates one complication (the weathering at Brekke, third paragraph) into the thesis. A is too strong, since the author says nothing shows imitative repair is always right, and E misplaces the critique, which targets the doctrine itself rather than one application of it.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that Solvang’s attitude toward imitative repair can best be described as one of
choices: indifference
disapproval
ambivalence
resignation
curiosity
questions.explanation: In the first paragraph Solvang calls imitative repair 'a quiet forgery' that misrepresents one age as another, a clear stance of disapproval (B). Nothing suggests he is torn about it (C) or accepts it as unavoidable (D); his whole doctrine is built to rule it out.

questions.stem: The primary function of the third paragraph is to
choices: recount the history of alterations to the building that the critic used as his principal example
present evidence that the critic’s recommended technique was carelessly executed at the building he admired
introduce the building traditions that are examined in more detail in the fourth paragraph
argue that most visitors to historic buildings take little interest in how those buildings were repaired
identify presuppositions of a view described in the first paragraph and indicate that one of them is not borne out by the critic’s own example
questions.explanation: The third paragraph names two 'undefended assumptions' (the evidentiary relationship and lasting visibility) and shows the second failing at Brekke, Solvang’s own model, which is E. B is the trap: the seam faded through weathering over forty years, not through careless work. A describes the second paragraph, and D overstates the paragraph, which identifies the evidentiary assumption without arguing that visitors are uninterested.

questions.stem: The passage raises all of the following as complications for Solvang’s doctrine EXCEPT:
choices: the expense of obtaining replacement materials that differ visibly from a building’s existing fabric
the tendency of contrasting new material to come to resemble the surrounding material over time
the existence of traditions in which faithful reproduction is understood as a form of continuity
the possibility that a conspicuous seam will lead viewers to infer an event that never occurred
the presence in many buildings of alterations made in several different periods
questions.explanation: Cost is never mentioned, so A is the exception. B is the weathering of the Brekke limestone (third paragraph), C is the Ise Shrine and Vestmark barns, D is the seam that suggests catastrophe where there was only maintenance (end of the fourth paragraph), and E is the point about the 1720s front and 1860s roof (second paragraph).

questions.stem: The passage suggests that Solvang’s position commits him to which one of the following views?
choices: The 1720s west front of the Brekke chapel should be treated as new work rather than as original fabric.
Imitative repair is acceptable when a building’s earlier alterations were themselves imitative.
Buildings that are rebuilt at regular intervals in the same form are exempt from the requirement that repairs be distinguishable.
Any future repair to the parts of the Brekke chapel rebuilt in the 1950s should be distinguishable from the 1950s work.
The work done on the Brekke chapel in the 1860s has less historical value than the work done in the 1950s.
questions.explanation: Solvang’s rule is that new work must be distinguishable from the existing fabric it repairs, and the second paragraph notes that the doctrine requires the latest intervention to announce itself. Once the 1950s work is itself old, a new repair to it must be set off from it as well, which is D. A is the trap: it echoes the author’s criticism, but the passage says Solvang in effect treated the 1720s front as though it were original, the opposite of A. C is the author’s complication, not Solvang’s commitment, and E confuses which work must announce itself with which work is more valuable.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to identify which one of the following as the primary reason that Solvang’s doctrine is ill suited to the stave barns of the Vestmark valley?
choices: The timber used in the barns weathers too quickly for any contrast between old and new boards to remain visible.
Those who maintain the barns understand them as tools to be kept in working order rather than as records to be read.
Unlike the Brekke chapel, the barns have no history of alterations made in earlier periods.
Imitative repair is in every case more faithful to a building’s past than distinguishable repair is.
The farmers who repair the barns lack the training needed to produce repairs in a contrasting manner.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says the farmers treat a barn as 'a tool to be kept in working order rather than a record to be consulted', and the last paragraph says whether a repair deceives depends on what the building is understood to be, so B. A borrows the weathering problem from the Brekke limestone, which the passage never applies to the barns. C is unsupported (board-by-board repair implies many alterations), and D contradicts the author’s statement that imitative repair is not always right.

questions.stem: With which one of the following statements would the author of the passage be most likely to agree?
choices: A repair that is plainly distinguishable from the surrounding fabric can nonetheless convey a misleading impression of a building’s history.
A repair that follows a local tradition of faithful reproduction cannot misrepresent a building’s past.
Conservation architects ought to abandon Solvang’s doctrine in favor of case-by-case judgment.
How a building should be repaired is a more fundamental question than what the building is understood to be.
Visitors to the Brekke chapel today can read its history more easily than visitors could in the 1950s.
questions.explanation: The end of the fourth paragraph says a conspicuous seam 'can mislead in its own way' by suggesting catastrophe where there was only routine maintenance, which supports A. B is the tempting trap, but the author says only that some traditions treat reproduction as continuity and adds that imitative repair is not always right; 'cannot misrepresent' goes beyond that. D reverses the author’s order of questions, and E reverses the weathering point, since the seam now needs a guide.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Because a rolling easement shifts title without compensation, the Calder High Court in Reyes sharply limited the circumstances in which the public easement may move.
Later surveys confirmed in every respect Judge Corran’s view that Ostrander had misapplied the law of river boundaries.
Distinctions drawn from the law of river boundaries cannot sensibly be applied to any coastline.

Calder’s rule tying movement of the public beach easement to the speed of shoreline change proved hard to apply and harmful to public access, and it was replaced by a test based on how long a change persists.
Despite the arbitrariness of its five-year period, the Reyes test has resolved each of the controversies that Ostrander provoked.
questions.explanation: The passage moves from the problem, through the Ostrander speed-based rule and its criticisms, to the 1996 survey and its replacement by the Reyes persistence test, which D captures. A gives the landowners’ objection, which the passage does not say motivated Reyes. B ('in every respect') and E ('each of the controversies') are too extreme, and E ignores the critics of Reyes in the last paragraph.

questions.stem: The author mentions a neighbor who lost the same thirty meters over twenty years (end of the second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: suggest that gradual erosion is more common on Calder’s coast than storm damage
indicate that the author regards the Ostrander rule as unfair to owners who lose land gradually
illustrate that the Ostrander rule treats equal losses of land differently depending on how rapidly they occurred
show that the Ostrander court misunderstood the law of river boundaries
present a case that the Reyes test would decide differently from the Ostrander rule
questions.explanation: The neighbor is paired with the hurricane-struck owner to show a concrete consequence of the rule: identical thirty-meter losses come out differently depending only on speed, which is C. B is tempting, but the author is describing how the rule works, not passing judgment, at that point. E fails because under Reyes a gradual shift that persists five years also moves the easement, so the neighbor’s case comes out the same.

questions.stem: The information in the passage most helps to answer which one of the following questions?
choices: Why did the Reyes court choose five years, rather than some other period, as its test of persistence?
How many Calder landowners sought compensation after the Ostrander decision?
Did courts in any other province adopt the rule announced in Ostrander?
What proportion of the sand fenced after Ostrander was eventually returned to public use?
What kind of event did the Ostrander court treat as an avulsion?
questions.explanation: The second paragraph defines avulsion as a sudden and perceptible loss 'such as that caused by a single storm', so E is answerable. A is the trap: the passage mentions critics who call the period arbitrary but never gives the court’s reason. D confuses sand that partly rebuilt naturally (fourth paragraph) with sand returned to public use, and B and C are never addressed.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information in the passage?
choices: Under the Reyes test, the public easement may come to cover sand that was exposed by a single storm.
Under the Ostrander rule, an owner whose vegetation line retreated gradually could fence the newly exposed sand.
The Reyes court adopted its test chiefly in response to landowners’ complaint that the easement shifted onto land they had never surrendered.
Under the Reyes test, the easement moves to a new vegetation line as soon as the line shifts.
Judge Corran maintained that the public easement should remain fixed regardless of how the shoreline changes.
questions.explanation: Reyes moves the easement whenever a shift persists five years 'however the shift occurred', so a storm-exposed strip that stays exposed would come under the easement, which is A. B reverses Ostrander, which let only storm-struck owners fence. D ignores the five-year requirement, and E reads more into Corran’s quoted objection to the river analogy than it says.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the objection to Ostrander raised by public access advocates, as described in the third paragraph?
choices: Many owners of beachfront parcels in Calder bought their land before the public’s customary right was recognized by the courts.
Sand stripped away by a storm is often partly restored by natural processes over the following months.
In the decades after Ostrander, most of the inland retreat of Calder’s vegetation line occurred during brief storms rather than through slow erosion.
The rate of gradual erosion along Calder’s coast increased substantially after 1979.
Courts in several neighboring provinces have declined to recognize any public right to use privately titled beaches.
questions.explanation: The advocates’ objection depends on the conditional premise that most land loss occurs in storms; C confirms it, so the avulsion exception would indeed cover most cases. D points the other way, since more gradual loss means more land over which the easement rolls. B is the geologists’ point and, if anything, suggests some storm losses are temporary, and A bears on the landowners’ objection rather than the advocates’.

questions.stem: Which one of the following statements about the Reyes test is most strongly supported by the passage?
choices: It answers the landowners’ objection that the easement could move onto land they had never surrendered.
It makes irrelevant a factual question that the coastal geologists mentioned in the third paragraph considered difficult to answer.
It moves the easement more promptly than the Ostrander rule did in cases of gradual erosion.
It was adopted by the court on the basis of the findings of the 1996 provincial survey.
It prevents landowners from fencing any portion of the sand exposed by a storm.
questions.explanation: The geologists doubted courts could tell gradual retreat from storm loss; Reyes asks only where the line has stood, 'not ... how quickly it got there' (last paragraph), so that question drops out, which is B. D is the strongest trap: the survey preceded Reyes and 'lent support' to the critics, but the passage never says the court relied on it. A fails because the easement still moves onto private land, and C reverses things, since Reyes waits for five years of persistence.

questions.stimulus: Parks director: Last spring, brighter lamps were installed along the walking paths in Fenwick Park. During the following summer, the park had nearly twice as many evening visitors as it had the summer before. Clearly, then, the brighter lamps are what drew the additional visitors to the park after dark.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the parks director's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: presumes that what is true of Fenwick Park must also be true of every other park in the city
relies on visitor counts that may have been gathered by people who favored the new lamps
overlooks the possibility that some other change could account for the increase in evening visitors
takes for granted that the lamps were installed in response to complaints from visitors
fails to establish that the additional visitors stayed in the park longer than earlier visitors did
questions.explanation: The director infers that the lamps caused the rise in evening visitors simply because the rise followed their installation, ignoring other possible causes such as a new event, warmer weather, or new nearby housing; C names this. A is tempting because such arguments often overgeneralize, but this one draws no conclusion about any other park. B, D, and E describe assumptions the argument never makes or needs.

questions.stimulus: Theater critic: The Harrow Playhouse should not abandon its practice of staging one new play by a local writer each season. Admittedly, these productions sell fewer tickets than the playhouse's revivals of familiar classics. But several plays that premiered at the Harrow have gone on to successful runs elsewhere, and that reputation for discovery is a major reason donors continue to support the playhouse.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the conclusion drawn in the argument?
choices: The Harrow Playhouse should continue staging one new play by a local writer each season.
The Harrow's productions of new local plays sell fewer tickets than its revivals of classics.
Several plays that premiered at the Harrow Playhouse have gone on to successful runs elsewhere.
Donors support the Harrow Playhouse mainly because of its reputation for discovering new plays.
The Harrow Playhouse should stage more new plays and fewer revivals of familiar classics.
questions.explanation: The first sentence is the conclusion: the playhouse should keep its practice of one new local play per season, and the rest of the stimulus concedes a cost and then gives reasons for keeping it, so A is correct. D distorts a premise (the critic says the reputation is 'a major reason,' not the main one), B is the conceded point, and E goes further than the critic, who argues only for keeping the current practice.

questions.stimulus: Ornithologists studying marsh wrens in the Teller Wetlands found that each male builds several dummy nests in addition to the nest in which eggs are laid. Building these extra nests costs the birds considerable time and energy. Yet wrens that build more dummy nests tend to raise more chicks than wrens that build fewer.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain how building dummy nests could increase the number of chicks a wren raises?
choices: Female wrens typically lay the same number of eggs regardless of how many nests the male has built.
Dummy nests are usually built from the same materials as the nests that hold eggs.
Wrens in the Teller Wetlands build more dummy nests in years when the insects they feed their chicks are plentiful.
Some other bird species in the Teller Wetlands also build nests that they never use.
Predators that find an empty dummy nest often stop searching the area before finding the nest with eggs.
questions.explanation: The stem asks how building dummy nests could itself lead to more chicks. E supplies a mechanism: dummy nests divert predators, so more eggs and chicks survive. C is the attractive trap, but it offers a different cause (plentiful food), suggesting the link is not causal, rather than explaining how the nests help; A, if anything, rules out one possible mechanism.

questions.stimulus: Nutritionist: In a survey of office workers, those who ate breakfast every day reported feeling more alert during morning meetings than did those who usually skipped breakfast. Hence, eating breakfast increases a person's alertness in the morning.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the nutritionist's argument?
choices: Many of the office workers surveyed drank coffee during their morning meetings.
Most of the surveyed workers who usually skipped breakfast also reported getting far less sleep than the breakfast eaters.
Some foods commonly eaten at breakfast contain more sugar than nutritionists recommend.
A few of the surveyed workers who ate breakfast every day reported feeling tired and distracted during their afternoon meetings at work.
Office workers who usually skip breakfast tend to eat a noticeably larger lunch than office workers who eat breakfast.
questions.explanation: The argument moves from a correlation to the claim that breakfast causes alertness. B offers an alternative cause: the breakfast skippers also sleep much less, which could explain their lower alertness. A would matter only if coffee drinking differed between the two groups, which it does not say; D concerns afternoons, and E concerns lunch.

questions.stimulus:
Ruiz: The Brookfield Public Library's main branch should stay open until 10 p.m. on weekdays. Many residents work until 6 p.m. or later, and the current 7 p.m. closing time leaves them almost no chance to use the library during the week.

Okafor: The library's budget is fixed, so longer hours would mean buying fewer new books. Residents who work late can still visit on Saturdays, and most of what the library offers is available online at any hour.
questions.stem: Ruiz and Okafor disagree over whether
choices: many Brookfield residents work until 6 p.m. or later
most of the library's offerings can be used online at any hour
residents who work late are able to visit the library on Saturdays
the library's main branch should stay open until 10 p.m. on weekdays
the library's budget should be increased to pay for keeping the main branch open longer
questions.explanation: Ruiz proposes the later weekday closing, and Okafor gives reasons against adopting it (fewer books, and other ways to use the library), so they disagree about D. Okafor never disputes that many residents work late (A), and Ruiz says nothing about online offerings (B) or Saturday visits (C); C is tempting because Okafor raises it, but Ruiz's complaint is specifically about weekdays. Neither proposes a larger budget (E).

questions.stimulus: At Linden Middle School's library, a student may borrow a laptop overnight only if the student has a signed permission form on file. Every student who has a signed permission form on file has also completed the library's device-care session. Rosa borrowed a laptop overnight last Tuesday.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Rosa has completed the library's device-care session.
Any student who has completed the device-care session may borrow a laptop overnight.
Rosa has borrowed a laptop overnight on more than one occasion.
Some students who have signed permission forms on file have never borrowed a laptop overnight.
Students without signed permission forms on file cannot borrow anything from the library.
questions.explanation: Rosa borrowed a laptop overnight, so she must have a signed form on file, and everyone with a signed form has completed the device-care session; hence A. B reverses the conditions: the session and the form are required for borrowing, not enough for it. E overextends a rule about laptops to all library items, and C and D are possible but not guaranteed.

questions.stimulus: Geologist: A layer of volcanic ash in the cliffs above Maren Bay matches, in chemical composition, the ash produced by an eruption of Mount Askel about 9,000 years ago. Therefore, the sediment layers lying directly beneath this ash in the cliffs were deposited more than about 9,000 years ago.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the geologist's argument?
choices: The eruption of Mount Askel was the largest eruption in the region in the last 9,000 years.
Ash from the Mount Askel eruption can be found at many sites besides Maren Bay.
No eruption much more recent than 9,000 years ago produced ash chemically identical to the Askel ash.
The sediment layers beneath the ash at Maren Bay were deposited at a steady rate.
Volcanic ash is the most reliable means geologists have for dating sediment layers.
questions.explanation: The argument dates the ash layer by its chemical match to the Askel eruption, so it requires that the match not have some other, later source. Negate C: if a much later eruption produced identical ash, the layer could be far younger, and the dating collapses. A is the tempting trap because size seems to matter, but the eruption need not be the largest for the match to identify it; B, D, and E are not needed.

questions.stimulus: Utility spokesperson: Last year Coralton Electric began sending some of its customers monthly reports comparing their electricity use with that of similar nearby households. Over the following year, customers who received the reports used 4 percent less electricity than they had the year before. So the reports led those customers to reduce their electricity use.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the spokesperson's argument?
choices: Electricity prices in Coralton's service area rose noticeably during the year in which the reports were first being sent out.
Many of the customers who received the reports said they found them confusing.
On average, customers who received the reports used more electricity than the similar households they were compared with.
Several other utilities have begun sending similar reports to their customers.
Customers randomly chosen not to receive the reports used about as much electricity as they had the year before.
questions.explanation: The argument attributes a drop in use to the reports, so it is vulnerable to other causes that would have reduced everyone's use. E supplies a control group: comparable customers without reports did not cut back, which makes the reports the likely cause. A is a trap that actually weakens by offering an alternative cause (higher prices), and C and D do not bear on whether the reports caused the drop.

questions.stimulus: After Dunmore County raised its minimum wage last year, employment at the county's restaurants did not decline. However, the average number of hours worked per restaurant employee fell by about 10 percent, and restaurants posted fewer job openings than in previous years. Over the same period, the rate at which restaurant employees quit their jobs dropped sharply.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: The increase in the minimum wage is what caused the county's restaurants to reduce the hours their employees worked.
Fewer employees leaving their jobs may account for part of the decline in the restaurants' job openings.
Restaurant employees in Dunmore County earned less in total last year than they had the year before.
The number of people employed at the county's restaurants rose after the minimum wage was increased.
Restaurants that reduced their employees' hours posted fewer job openings than other restaurants did.
questions.explanation: Job openings arise largely when workers leave, so a sharp drop in quitting gives a plausible partial explanation for fewer openings; B's hedged claim is well supported. A is the tempting trap, but the facts show only that hours fell after the wage rose, not that the wage increase caused it. C cannot be determined without knowing how much hourly pay rose, D goes beyond 'did not decline,' and E compares restaurants the facts never distinguish.

questions.stimulus: Council member Ibsen argues that the city should close the dog run in Larkspur Park because too few residents use it to justify what it costs to maintain. Yet Ibsen's own figures show that more residents use the dog run each week than use the park's tennis courts, which cost even more to maintain, and Ibsen has argued for keeping the tennis courts. So Ibsen's argument for closing the dog run should be rejected.
questions.stem: The argument proceeds by
choices: questioning the accuracy of the figures on which Ibsen bases a proposal
arguing that a facility should be kept because it is more popular than any other facility in the park
criticizing Ibsen's motives rather than the substance of Ibsen's proposal
showing that the reasoning behind Ibsen's proposal, if applied consistently, would support a conclusion that Ibsen rejects
proposing a different way to reduce the cost of maintaining the park's facilities
questions.explanation: The arguer accepts Ibsen's figures and points out that Ibsen's standard (low use relative to cost justifies closing) would condemn the tennis courts even more, yet Ibsen wants to keep them; that is D. B is tempting, but the argument compares the dog run only with the tennis courts and does not claim it is the most popular facility. A is wrong because the argument relies on Ibsen's figures rather than disputing them.

questions.stimulus: Energy analyst: Ten years ago, rooftop solar panels generated 5 percent of the electricity used by households in Velmont. Today they generate 9 percent. So Velmont households now use less electricity from sources other than rooftop solar than they did ten years ago.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the energy analyst's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: takes for granted that a trend observed over the past decade will continue at the same pace into the next
ignores that a smaller percentage of a larger total can exceed a larger percentage of a smaller one
assumes without justification that rooftop solar panels are less costly than other sources of electricity
treats evidence about electricity used by households as though it applied to businesses as well
fails to consider whether households in other towns have experienced a similar trend
questions.explanation: The non-solar share fell from 95 to 91 percent, but if total household use rose by more than about 4.4 percent, the amount drawn from non-solar sources actually increased; B describes this percent-versus-amount error. A is tempting, but the conclusion is about the present, not a prediction. D describes a confusion the argument never makes, since it concerns only households, and C and E raise matters the conclusion does not depend on.

questions.stimulus: Ecologist: Gray shrikes in the Ostrava Hills impale the insects they catch on thorns before eating them. One grasshopper species common in the hills carries a toxin that breaks down within two days after the insect dies. Shrikes eat most impaled prey within a few hours, but they leave impaled grasshoppers of this species on the thorns for two days or more before eating them. Thus, ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the ecologist's argument?
choices: shrikes impale prey on thorns chiefly in order to make toxic prey safe to eat
the toxin carried by these grasshoppers is harmful to most bird species
shrikes would eat more of these grasshoppers if their toxin broke down more quickly
shrikes in the Ostrava Hills catch more grasshoppers than any other kind of prey
the shrikes' practice of impaling prey may help protect them from the grasshoppers' toxin
questions.explanation: Shrikes wait just long enough for the toxin to break down before eating these grasshoppers, so impaling, which lets them store the prey, plausibly protects them from the toxin, as E cautiously states. A overreaches with 'chiefly': shrikes impale all their prey, most of which they eat within hours, so detoxifying cannot be the main purpose. B, C, and D go beyond anything the facts establish.

questions.stimulus: Principal: Any course that requires students to complete a substantial independent research project develops students' ability to evaluate sources. Every course in Fairview High School's new humanities sequence requires such a project. Therefore, every course in the new humanities sequence should count toward the school's information-literacy requirement.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the principal's argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Any course that develops students' ability to evaluate sources should count toward the school's information-literacy requirement.
Only courses that develop students' ability to evaluate sources should count toward the school's information-literacy requirement.
Students who complete independent research projects evaluate sources better than students who do not.
Every course that counts toward the information-literacy requirement requires a substantial independent research project.
Most courses outside the new humanities sequence do not develop students' ability to evaluate sources.
questions.explanation: The premises establish that every course in the sequence develops students' ability to evaluate sources; A links that property to counting toward the requirement, so the conclusion follows. B is the attractive trap but reverses the needed conditional: it makes source evaluation necessary for counting, not sufficient. D likewise reverses direction, and C and E do not connect the courses to the requirement.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: The Dalby Cannery cut its workers' hourly wages last month, citing recent losses. But two years ago, when the workers agreed to forgo a scheduled raise, the owners promised that wages would not be reduced so long as the cannery remained profitable over each full year. The cannery made a profit last year despite its losses in recent months. So the wage cut was unjustified.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, would most help to justify the columnist's argument?
choices: An employer that asks its workers to forgo a scheduled raise should fully explain the financial reasons behind the request.
Wage reductions are justified only when they are genuinely needed to keep a company from going out of business.
Workers who make a concession in exchange for an employer's promise are owed that promise whenever its stated conditions are met.
A company's owners may reduce wages whenever the company's monthly costs exceed its monthly revenue, regardless of its annual results.
Promises that employers make during labor negotiations are binding only if they have been put in writing.
questions.explanation: The columnist's case rests on the promise: workers gave up a raise, the promised condition (a profitable full year) held, so cutting wages broke the promise; C states exactly that principle. B is tempting, but nothing in the argument says the cut was not needed to keep the cannery open, so B could not establish the conclusion. D supports the cannery, and E would undercut the columnist unless the promise was written, which is not stated.

questions.stimulus: Every film shown at the Corvo Festival this year was chosen by the festival's selection jury, and the jury chose no film that had already been released commercially. The Long Field has already been released commercially, so it was not shown at the Corvo Festival this year.
questions.stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following arguments is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Every car sold at Henley Motors is inspected by Pratt, and Pratt inspects no car that has more than 100,000 miles on it. So the sedan Pratt inspected last week has fewer than 100,000 miles on it.
Every member of the choir auditioned for the director, and the director turned away no one who could read music. Since Lin can read music, Lin is a member of the choir.
All of the paintings in the east gallery were donated by Ames, and Ames donated no painting made before 1900. The Tolland portrait was made before 1900, so Ames did not donate it.
Every dish on the Corbel Café's lunch menu is prepared by its head chef, and the head chef prepares no dish that contains peanuts. The café's satay contains peanuts, so it is not on the lunch menu.
Every book in the reading room was approved by the librarian, and the librarian approves only books in good condition. This atlas is in good condition, so it must be in the reading room.
questions.explanation: The argument chains two rules (shown at the festival → chosen by the jury; chosen by the jury → not released commercially) and, from an item lacking the final property, concludes by contrapositive that it lacks the first: it was not shown. D matches step for step: the satay contains peanuts, so the chef did not prepare it, so it is not on the menu. C is the most tempting trap, but it concludes only that the painting was not donated by Ames, never using the gallery premise to reach a conclusion about the gallery; A runs forward from the middle term, and B and E reverse the conditionals.

questions.stimulus: For decades, groundwater has been pumped heavily for irrigation in the Halden Valley, and as a result the land surface over most of the valley has sunk by more than a meter. In recent years, pumping has continued at the same rate and the water table has kept falling just as fast as before, yet the land has been sinking much more slowly than it did earlier.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: In recent years, rainfall in the Halden Valley has been greater than its long-term average.
Land sinks when the removal of groundwater allows underground layers of fine clay to compact under the weight of the material above them.
Several farms in the valley have recently switched to irrigation methods that use less water.
In a neighboring valley where less groundwater is pumped, the land has sunk by only a few centimeters.
Most of the clay beneath the valley has already compacted almost as far as it can, and the sands that remain barely compact.
questions.explanation: The puzzle is why unchanged pumping and an equally fast-falling water table now produce less sinking. E explains it: the compressible clay has largely finished compacting, and the remaining sands barely compact. B is the tempting trap: it explains why pumping causes sinking at all but not why the sinking has slowed; A and C conflict with the stated facts that the water table and pumping rate are unchanged.

questions.stimulus: Dietitian: This year Westbrook Elementary began offering free fruit at lunch, and on average its students now eat fewer cookies and chips at lunch than they did last year. Clearly, offering free fruit leads children to eat fruit in place of snack foods.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions would be most useful in evaluating the dietitian's argument?
choices: Do Westbrook students prefer some kinds of fruit, such as apples, to other kinds offered at lunch?
Did students at comparable schools without free fruit also eat fewer cookies and chips at lunch this year?
Is fruit generally more nutritious for growing children than cookies and chips are?
How much does it cost Westbrook each year to provide free fruit to students at lunch?
Do Westbrook students eat more cookies and chips at home after school than they did last year?
questions.explanation: The dietitian credits the fruit program for a drop in snack eating, so the key question is whether something else, such as a district-wide change, caused the drop. If comparable schools without free fruit saw the same decline, the program looks irrelevant; if not, the argument is strengthened, so B is useful either way. E is tempting, but the conclusion concerns what children eat at lunch, not at home, and A, C, and D do not bear on the causal claim.

questions.stimulus: Parks official: Critics say that replacing the lawn in Orchard Square with native meadow plants was a mistake because the square now draws fewer visitors. But the meadow has cut the square's water use by 60 percent, and in a survey posted on the square's information board, 85 percent of respondents said they approve of the meadow. So the change has been popular with the public.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most undermines the parks official's defense?
choices: Most people who stopped visiting the square after the meadow was planted did so because they preferred the lawn.
The meadow requires more frequent maintenance work by park staff than the old lawn did, which raises the square's labor costs.
Several other cities have replaced lawns in public squares with native plants.
Many of the people who responded to the survey also visit other parks in the city.
Some survey respondents said they would like benches added to the meadow.
questions.explanation: The survey reached only people who still come to the square, so it leaves out exactly those most likely to dislike the change. A confirms that the people who stopped coming did so because they disliked the meadow, so the 85 percent figure does not reflect the public as a whole. B is the tempting trap: it supports the critics' view that the change was a mistake, but it does not touch the official's conclusion that the change is popular.

questions.stimulus: Film historian: Records show that the silent film The Lantern Keeper was shown in only three cities during its original release, and few reviews of it were published. Yet its distinctive camera techniques appear in dozens of films by directors who began working in the years just after its release. These directors, then, must have seen The Lantern Keeper.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the film historian's argument depends?
choices: Most of the directors who used the techniques lived in or near one of the three cities where the film was shown.
The few published reviews of The Lantern Keeper praised its camera techniques.
The directors who used the techniques were more innovative than most other directors of their time.
The techniques were not described in some widely available publication before those directors began using them.
The Lantern Keeper was seen by more people than the surviving records indicate.
questions.explanation: The historian infers from shared techniques that the directors must have seen the film, which requires ruling out other ways they could have learned the techniques. Negate D: if a widely available publication described the techniques, the directors could have learned them there, and 'must have seen' fails. A and E are attractive because they would make it easier for the directors to have seen the film, but the argument does not need either: a film shown in only three cities could still have reached these directors.

questions.stimulus: A utility should postpone shutting off a household's service for nonpayment whenever the household has made at least one partial payment within the past sixty days and, in addition, either someone in the household depends on electrically powered medical equipment or temperatures are forecast to fall below freezing during the following week.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: The Garcias' last partial payment was ninety days ago, but Mr. Garcia relies on a home oxygen machine, so the utility should postpone shutting off their service.
The Whitfields made a partial payment two weeks ago, and no one in the household uses medical equipment; with mild weather forecast, the utility should postpone shutting off their service.
The Lees made a partial payment last month, and a hard freeze is forecast for next week, so the utility should postpone shutting off their service.
The Novaks have made no partial payments this year, although Ms. Novak relies on a powered wheelchair, so the utility is required to shut off their service.
The Ortegas made a partial payment last month and rely on medical equipment, so the utility should not only postpone shutting off their service but also forgive their unpaid balance.
questions.explanation: The principle requires a partial payment within sixty days plus either medical-equipment dependence or a forecast freeze. The Lees meet both parts, so C conforms. D is the subtle trap: the Novaks fail the payment condition, but the principle says only when a shutoff should be postponed, not when one is required; A fails the sixty-day condition, B meets neither of the second conditions, and E adds forgiveness, which the principle never addresses.

questions.stimulus: Conservationist: Any bird species in the Pellam Islands whose nests are within reach of the introduced rats is in danger of local extinction unless it breeds more than once a year. Every bird species in danger of local extinction there should be included in the new captive-breeding program. The Pellam rail nests only on the ground, where the rats can reach its nests. So the Pellam rail should be included in the captive-breeding program.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the conservationist's argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Only bird species whose nests are within reach of the rats should be included in the captive-breeding program.
The Pellam rail breeds less often than any other bird species in the Pellam Islands.
Any bird species that breeds only once a year is in danger of local extinction if rats can reach its nests.
Every bird species in the Pellam Islands that nests only on the ground breeds more than once a year.
Every bird species in the Pellam Islands that breeds more than once a year nests at least partly off the ground.
questions.explanation: The rail's nests are within the rats' reach, so it is endangered (and belongs in the program) unless it breeds more than once a year; the argument needs to rule that out. By contrapositive, E says that a species nesting only on the ground does not breed more than once a year, which completes the chain. B is the most attractive trap, but breeding less often than every other species is compatible with breeding twice a year; C restates part of the first rule without saying how often the rail breeds, and D would defeat the conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Most of the breakfast cereals sold at Grantham Market are fortified with iron, and most of the iron-fortified cereals sold there are high in sugar. So most of the breakfast cereals sold at Grantham Market are high in sugar.
questions.stem: The pattern of questionable reasoning in the argument above is most similar to that in which one of the following?
choices: Most of the employees at Dorrit Mills work the night shift, and every night-shift employee there receives a wage premium. So most of the employees at Dorrit Mills receive a wage premium.
Most of the trails in Kessel Forest are open to cyclists, and most of the forest's trails that are open to cyclists are steep. So most of the trails in Kessel Forest are steep.
Most of the novels on Ingrid's shelf are mysteries, and most mysteries are set in cities. So it is likely that at least one novel on Ingrid's shelf is set in a city.
Most of the students in Pell's class passed the exam, and most of those who passed had studied with a tutor. So most of the students who studied with a tutor passed the exam.
Most of the members of the Arden Hiking Club are retired, and the club's president is a member. So the club's president is probably retired.
questions.explanation: The argument chains two 'most' statements, but most of a majority need not be a majority of the whole (60 percent of 60 percent is only 36 percent). B makes the identical error with trails, cyclists, and steepness. A is the strongest trap because it looks the same, but its second premise says 'every,' which makes the conclusion valid; D commits a different error, reversing which group is said to be 'most' of which, while C and E draw modest, reasonable probabilistic conclusions.

questions.stimulus: Granite boulders scattered across the Tamsin Plain are of a type found in place only in the Dovre Mountains, 200 kilometers to the north. Geologists know of only two processes able to carry boulders that far: glaciers and catastrophic floods. Boulders carried by floods are rounded and smoothed, whereas boulders carried by glaciers typically keep sharp edges and often bear parallel scratches. Most of the Dovre granite boulders on the plain have sharp edges, though a few are rounded.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: At least some of the Dovre granite boulders on the Tamsin Plain were carried there by glaciers.
All of the Dovre granite boulders on the Tamsin Plain were carried there by a single glacier.
The rounded boulders on the Tamsin Plain were carried there by catastrophic floods.
Most of the Dovre granite boulders on the Tamsin Plain bear parallel scratches.
No catastrophic flood has ever swept from the Dovre Mountains to the Tamsin Plain.
questions.explanation: Flood-carried boulders are rounded, so the many sharp-edged boulders could not have come by flood; since only glaciers and floods could carry them, those boulders were carried by glaciers, as A says. C is the tempting trap: glacier-carried boulders only 'typically' keep sharp edges, so the few rounded ones could also have arrived by glacier. B and E ignore the rounded boulders' uncertain origin, and D overstates 'often bear' scratches.

questions.stimulus: Economist: Two years after the town of Ashby began requiring employers to list salary ranges in job postings, the gap between the average starting salaries of men and women hired by Ashby firms had narrowed considerably. The requirement probably narrowed the gap by giving applicants, many of whom had previously had little idea what a position paid, a firmer basis for negotiating their pay.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the economist's argument?
choices: Since the requirement took effect, far more women than before have applied for positions at Ashby firms of every size.
Some Ashby employers listed salary ranges in their job postings even before the requirement took effect.
Job postings in Ashby that list salary ranges attract more applicants than postings that do not.
The gap narrowed mainly for positions whose starting pay was individually negotiated, and hardly at all for positions with fixed pay scales.
Women hired by Ashby firms since the requirement took effect have, on average, more work experience than women hired before it.
questions.explanation: The economist claims both that the requirement narrowed the gap and that it did so by aiding negotiation. D fits that mechanism precisely: the gap shrank where pay is negotiated and not where pay is fixed, which is hard to explain unless the change worked through negotiation. A is tempting because more female applicants sounds favorable, but a changed applicant pool is an alternative explanation, not support; E likewise offers an alternative cause (more experienced hires), and B, if anything, slightly weakens.

questions.stimulus: Library board member: Advocates of eliminating overdue fines at Corland's public libraries claim that doing so would increase the number of books borrowed, and they cite a pilot program at the Wexley branch, where borrowing rose after fines were dropped. But the pilot coincided with the opening of a large school next door to the Wexley branch, which by itself could have increased borrowing there. So eliminating overdue fines would not increase the number of books borrowed.
questions.stem: The board member's reasoning is flawed in that the argument
choices: attacks the motives of those who advocate eliminating overdue fines rather than addressing their evidence
relies on a possible explanation of the pilot results without considering whether the new school's students use the library
takes the weakness of the evidence offered for a claim as sufficient grounds for concluding that the claim is false
presumes that an increase in borrowing is the only reason anyone has offered for eliminating overdue fines
assumes that the results of a pilot program at one branch cannot reveal anything about the effects of a citywide policy
questions.explanation: The board member legitimately shows that the Wexley pilot does not establish its conclusion, since the new school is an uncontrolled alternative cause, but then concludes that eliminating fines would not increase borrowing; discrediting the evidence for a claim does not show the claim false, as C says. B is the main trap: offering a possible alternative explanation is enough to undercut the pilot as evidence, so the member need not prove the school's students borrow. D is also tempting, but the argument concerns only borrowing and presumes nothing about other reasons, and E misdescribes the objection, which concerns a confounding event rather than the limits of pilots.
